opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and honestly one I think about a lot. I think in two years, the basic idea will probably still be useful, but how we measure it will have to change a fair amount.

The core insight behind time horizon is that you can put very different tasks on a common scale: how long would it take a skilled human to do this, and at what length of task does the model succeed about half the time? That framing is nice because it's intuitive, it's comparable across models and over time, and it connects fairly directly to the things people actually care about, like how much autonomous work you can hand off to these systems.

The practical challenge is that if trends roughly continue, and so far they've held up surprisingly well with a doubling time of several months, then in two years we're talking about models whose fifty-percent horizons might be measured in days or even weeks of human-expert work. Building and validating tasks at that length is really hard. You need human baselines, and getting a skilled professional to spend a week on a task, many times over, under controlled conditions, is expensive and slow. So I expect we'll lean more on things like estimating task length without full baselines, decomposing long tasks, or using naturally occurring work, such as real software projects with known completion times.

I also think there'll be more attention on the gap between benchmark-style tasks and messy real-world work. Our tasks are fairly well specified and automatically scorable, and we've seen hints that models do worse on messier tasks with less clear feedback. So one direction is time horizon on more realistic distributions, and seeing whether the trend lines look similar or quite different.

And then there's the question of what it's used for. Right now it's partly a forecasting tool and partly a way of communicating progress. In two years, I'd guess it gets used more directly in safety and governance contexts, as one input into questions like "could this model meaningfully accelerate AI R&D?" For that, you care less about the headline number and more about horizons on specific, high-stakes task distributions, and about reliability at higher success thresholds, not just fifty percent.

So, short answer: I think the concept sticks around, but the measurement gets harder, more domain-specific, and more tied to real-world work, and we'll have to be pretty careful about how far we extrapolate.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that measurement will become more domain-specific and depend on task distributions and reliability thresholds, rather than relying on a single headline horizon.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's worth separating two things here. There's time horizon as a metric that METR actually measures, where you take a bunch of tasks, you figure out how long they take humans, and you find the task length at which models succeed 50% of the time or 80% of the time. And then there's time horizon as a sort of conceptual frame that people use when they talk about AI progress, like "models can now do tasks that take humans a day" or "a week."

My honest expectation is that the conceptual frame is going to stick around and probably get more popular, and the specific measurement is going to get harder and harder to do well. Those two things are kind of in tension.

On the measurement side, the basic problem is that if horizons keep doubling every seven months or so, and you're already at tasks that take humans several hours, in two years you're talking about tasks that take humans weeks or months. And it's just really hard to build a benchmark of week-long tasks. You need to actually have humans do them to get your baselines, which is extremely expensive, and the number of people who can do a given month-long task well is small. The tasks also become much less self-contained. A real month-long project involves talking to people, changing your mind about what the goal even was, waiting for things. Our tasks are mostly "here's a well-specified problem, go," and I think that becomes a more and more distorted picture of what real work looks like the longer the task gets.

So I'd guess in two years you'll see a few things. One is that the headline number will probably still get reported, but with much wider error bars and more caveats, and I'd expect the field to have moved toward reporting things like 80% horizons or reliability-conditioned horizons rather than just 50%, because the 50% number increasingly says "the model can sometimes pull this off" rather than "you can rely on this." Two, I think you'll see people decompose it more, so instead of one number you'll have horizons for software engineering, for ML research, for agentic computer use, and those will diverge. The software one has been racing ahead partly because that's where the training signal is. Three, I think there'll be more effort on measuring horizon in the wild, like looking at what tasks people actually successfully delegate to models in real deployments, rather than on constructed task suites. That's messier but it addresses the self-containedness problem.

And then the thing I'd flag as a risk is that the metric is pretty legible, which is great for communication and kind of dangerous for interpretation. It's very easy to draw the line out and say "in 2028 they'll do year-long tasks," and I think the actual relationship between benchmark horizon and real-world capability is going to get weaker, not stronger, as the tasks get longer. So I'd expect it to be used a lot in two years, I'd expect it to still be one of the more informative single numbers we have, and I'd expect the people most worried about it to be the people who produce it.

r001.rationale: The response predicts a shift toward 80% or reliability-conditioned horizons and separate horizons by task domain, so it expects measurements to be conditioned or scaled by factors beyond the basic time-horizon number.

astra-6.text:
My guess is that it’ll still be a useful measure, but we’ll be more careful about specifying what it measures. The length of a task isn’t the only thing that determines how hard it is for an AI. A task can take a human a long time because it involves a lot of repetitive work, or because it requires a single really difficult insight. Those are quite different capability requirements.

So I’d expect more emphasis on things like: in what domain, with what tools, with how much human assistance, and at what success rate? Being able to complete a long task occasionally is very different from being able to do it reliably enough that someone can delegate it.

In two years, I could imagine time horizon being a standard headline number, but I’d hope it comes with those qualifications. The thing we ultimately want to understand is how much useful work you can hand off to a system and trust it to finish. Time horizon gives us one way of getting at that, but I wouldn’t expect a single number to capture the whole picture.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that time-horizon numbers will be qualified by domain, tools, human assistance, and success rate, indicating that measurements will account for other factors.

sol-6.1.text:
My guess is that it’ll be one of the standard ways people describe what a model can do, but there’ll be a lot of work going into figuring out exactly what the number means.

The attractive thing about time horizon is that it connects performance to something people have an intuition for: can this system do a task that would take a human ten minutes, an hour, or a day? That’s useful in a way that getting a few more percentage points on a benchmark often isn’t.

But I don’t think you’ll be able to characterize a system with a single horizon. It matters which tasks you’re measuring, which humans you’re comparing against, what tools the system has, and how reliably it has to succeed. A system that completes half of the tasks that take a human a day could still be quite frustrating to delegate work to.

So in two years, I’d expect people to report time horizons more routinely, ideally at several reliability levels and across different domains. And I’d expect a lot of the interesting discussion to be about how those measurements translate into useful work. Can you hand the system something, come back later, and trust that it’s done? Time horizon gives us a way to start answering that, but it doesn’t answer it by itself.

r001.rationale: The response expects time horizons to be reported across domains and at several reliability levels, and says other factors affect characterization. It does not predict that the measurements will be weighted or scaled according to those factors.
